utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Josse and Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution composition, as yesterday, Mr. McCloskey, Vanderpuye and Ms. Soljan. Good morning to you, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hopefully, you should be out of this room before us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manning. How are you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yesterday, I was questioning you and drew an objection from the Prosecution about Mr. Haglund, who is your friend and who you highly respect. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We have in evidence the report of the Oversight Committee, and it's 2D70. I don't know whether we need to put it on e-court right now. Certainly, we can. It was completed November 15th and 16th, 1997. Now, does that ring any bells with you? Before you started.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the Oversight Committee term. I know there was a document in relation to, as you described yesterday, allegations in relation to the 1996 exhumations. I'm assuming that's the same document, without seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And so you weren't aware, then, that the questions concerning specific allegations, including -- included but were not limited to the methods of collection and chain of custody, problems in body count and possible loss of chain of custody of bones, coordination of operations between anthropology and pathology, and changing the cause and manner of death again after the Prosecutor had departed and had never been notified of those changes. You'd never heard of these allegations; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was aware of allegations having been made which had been made prior to my arrival at the Tribunal. I was aware that there was a document. I'm sure I read the document. Since that time, it's of no great consequence to me. I'm sure I've read the document. I can't recall it in detail now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 4 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Manning, do you see it in front of you? Scroll up. There you go.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a document which has a subtitle -- subparagraph of "6", "Pre-investigative comments."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And comment 5, have you ever heard of Clyde Snow?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I've met Dr. Snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And you can see and you can read paragraph 5 there, that Clyde Snow felt at times it was Dr. Haglund versus the UNTAES, and many bodies removed in one day. Dr. Snow stated in his opinion no more than 20 bodies should have been exhumed in any single day. He felt Dr. Haglund showed "very poor judgement," and it was lucky nothing had "blown up" as a result of the procedures used. Now, Mr. Manning, you know that Clyde Snow is a preeminent forensic anthropologist, do you not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've met Dr. Snow and I've seen some of his papers. I don't know his standing, but there's nothing to indicate that he is not in good standing in the community, but I didn't deal with him. But certainly I know that he's a pathologist and well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And of course you've not read any of the transcripts of Dr. Petrucelli, Dr. Baraybar, Dr. Wright, Dr. Lawrence; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these proceedings, I have read no transcripts, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And are you aware that Dr. Baraybar and Dr. Petrucelli indicated, from this witness stand, that they believe Dr. Clyde Snow is a most preeminent figure in the forensic anthropology world?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have access to any testimony and I hadn't discussed it with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Further, you see that he's obviously stated there was sloppy science in these digs in 1996. Do you see that under paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can see that written.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now Can we turn to the next page, please. Focus it on 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This is a question that drew an objection yesterday. David Del Pino, a Chilean anthropologist, stated that: "The operations were halted when Dr. Haglund was away. Clothing was discarded at Haglund's command, even though some contained identification. Forms were not always used, and there was no delegation of authority." Now, obviously you weren't there, and you can't say whether or not these allegations are true or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't there. I had nothing to do with this document or these discussions. I would say that I reviewed all the material produced from 1996 from Dr. Haglund's report. And from the records that I saw, I saw nothing to indicate specific wide-ranging problems. There were, as in every exhumation or every endeavour of this size, some misnumbering, some mislabelling, some general errors, but in my review of the material, I didn't see any glaring errors or problems or issues. And, in fact, I saw some fairly detailed and comprehensive records and notes produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you agree, though, with the complaint that we talked about earlier, that changing the cause and manner of death, after the Prosecutor had departed, had never been notified of these changes, could be a very real problem, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I really understand the Prosecutor departing. I can see the reference in the document, but I don't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If I can -- I may draw an objection, but I think what they indicated here was Kirschner had other pathologists working under him, and they would give a cause of death and then depart, and he would just take it and change it without notifying them or questioning or asking them.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not aware of that happening, and if you're asking me if that's incorrect, I would suggest that that's an incorrect process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, this committee even found -- and, again, it would be under page 10. Scroll up a little bit for Roman numeral IX. Do you see that discussion, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read that section?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: To yourself.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read that, that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And even the opinions and comments by Dr. Vincent De Maio, which is just a paragraph above Roman numeral IX where it states: "While Dr. Kirschner's actions had the potential to invalidate or at least taint the autopsy reports, the Tribunal prevented this by submitting the reports back to the original physicians for their certification of cause and manner of death."

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you can see that this committee was so concerned that they even thought about bringing possible criminal charges or licensing charges of ethical violations by Kirschner. Do you see that under IX?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see discussion as possibilities or options. Again, I'd like to say that I wasn't involved in this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So you really can't comment because you weren't involved with it; right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Effectively, I didn't deal with these allegations, I didn't discuss it with these people, so I have difficulty in providing information in relation to this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And wouldn't it be just logically the same, that you really didn't have any involvement in the process of the ICMP and their DNA analysis, so you really can't even comment on that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that's the case. I used the data provided by ICMP. I had attended ICMP's premises, reviewed their processes, spoke to the people involved, reviewed the files, and examined the data held by the Bosnian Court as well as the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. I had no involvement with this document that you're putting to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And although you testified that you probably recall reading that document at some point?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just like you read the things that ICMP put out; correct? "Yes" or "no," so we can finish this.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Did -- you mentioned yesterday that you had talked to many people to uphold your opinion that every single person in these graves died as a result of a murder or execution; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd spoken to a number of people in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: One of them was Dr. Petrucelli; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you give us approximate time period, year, month, that you may have talked to Dr. Petrucelli?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was involved directly with the exhumations conducted by Mr. Petrucelli over several months. I also dealt with him at the Tribunal when he was preparing to give evidence, and I think I may have seen and met and spoke with him over three years. I can't give you an indication. We certainly discussed -- we certainly discussed the exhumation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, again, prior to the 13th day of March of 2007, when was the last time that you spoke to him about the exhumation process?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the last time that I spoke to Mr. Petrucelli was perhaps 2002, maybe earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you'd indicated yesterday that part of your discussion concerned the cause and manner of death; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I also indicated that I believed that was contained in his report or reports, but that I would have to check those specific reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You weren't here, obviously you haven't read the transcript, but on the 13th day of March, he was being questioned, Dr. Petrucelli, and on page 8763 of this transcript, and he was asked, line 6, question: "All right. Well, were you ever, in the context of your professional capacity, at Ravnice, were you ever asked to provide an opinion to Dean Manning about how you considered these persons to have met their death?" Answer: "No." Is that right, Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present for the testimony, so I assume that's what Mr. Petrucelli said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Shall we believe Mr. Petrucelli, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that that's more than possible that he didn't provide an opinion. We discussed it, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Mr. Manning is not to comment on this. It's characterising other witnesses' testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, he said yesterday under oath that Dr. Petrucelli, and also today, had talked to him about the cause and manner of death, the specific, and I'm asking him whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's bring this to a close. Your question was a very straightforward one, "Shall we believe Mr. Petrucelli," and Ms. Soljan is perfectly right. You can't ask another witness whether, according to him, we should believe another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I was trying to refresh his recollection, Your Honour, but I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's better, and also I think you should come to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, since you've been a police officer of 24 years and the majority of those years were in Australia, frankly, I don't know the Criminal Code there, but do you have something that we call in America "the Miranda warnings"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not trying to be pedantic. I spent about nine and a half years overseas in that service. Yes, we have a Miranda. We call it a caution, a criminal caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when you came here in 1998 and became an investigator, were there protocols in place that you learned or were told to use, as an investigator, to interview suspects?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a process in relation to interviewing witnesses and suspects that did progress and adapt as the Tribunal moved on, but there was a set of instructions, and I think there still is a set of instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall part of that instruction being that if a person you were interviewing was considered to be a suspect, that he needed to be given certain warnings?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The process would have been that the suspect, if he was considered a suspect, would have been cautioned, depending perhaps on the circumstances. There are some conversations which might not be conducted in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Also, you're aware of the Rules of the Tribunal, are you not, that anyone considered to be a suspect and being questioned by the OTP, that that discussion must be tape-recorded or audio-recorded; are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am aware of that, although I think, and I have not been here for some years, that there's a clause that if it's not practical or available or similar, but generally they should be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you ever, sir, been taught or trained here that when you had a individual who had been summonsed as a suspect, that it was appropriate to tell them in their warnings that, "We believe that you are a possible suspect," instead of "a suspect"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you don't believe, do you, sir, that that would be correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a difficult question to answer without specific circumstances or specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll give you one, then. Individual A has been summonsed by your office, and the summons says, "You are a suspect --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did he interview any suspects?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you interview any suspects, sir, any suspects?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In relation to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In relation to this case.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I interviewed a number of people, some of whom were suspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And suspect A has been -- and these ones you interviewed as suspects had received summons, correct, to come talk to you at the Banja Luka office or wherever it might be?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individuals were summonsed to the interview process, but I can't recall if that automatically made them suspects. I don't believe so. We would summons individuals to attend for interview via the system that was in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you don't recall a time that if a person that you wanted to interview, you consider him a suspect, that that was not put in the summons that he received?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that if they were a suspect, they would have been given a different summons process, but again this is some four or five years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, again, if you had -- were going to interview a person who you, as an investigator, knew was a suspect, would you ever tell them, in their warnings, "Mr. A, you are a possible suspect and you have the right to ...," whatever, after that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it would depend on the circumstances, but I could envisage using the word "possible suspect."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Why would that be, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, given the circumstances, it could be that the person is borderline, you don't even know if it's the right person. You started the conversation with the person. It's difficult, without a specific circumstance, to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. How many people did you interview in regards to this case, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including witnesses, between 60 and a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall interviewing a Ostoja Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes. If you could tell me what area he was employed in. I think engineering?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Branko Ilic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check my records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Damjan Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Milorad Bircakovic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bircakovic. I believe so, but again I'd have to check the records. They're familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Ljubo Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Dragan Markovic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, possible. I could check the records. If I interviewed them, there was a record made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if, again, the Rules of the Tribunal while you were operating were that all conversations with suspects should be tape-recorded, you followed that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed the rules that were in place at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And so you wouldn't ever have any off-the-record conversations with these suspects, would you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you would have to give me specific circumstances, but generally if a person is a suspect, considered a suspect by the Tribunal, that person -- the interview should be conducted on tape and recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the reasons obviously are to protect not only the person giving the statement, but the interviewers like yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's part of the reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. What are some other reasons?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're interviewing a suspect, to ensure that there is a complete and accurate record of the conversation, perhaps to present into court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, do you recall on 25 November 2001 interviewing Dragan Jevtic at the United Nations headquarters in Banja Luka on 25 November, 2001, a Sunday?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, if you could tell me what unit he was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could I have the help of the usher for just a minute with the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, while that's getting set up, can you tell us briefly, under what circumstances would you have a conversation off the record with a suspect?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe I would. Perhaps if the accused -- or, sorry, the suspect had his legal counsel there and a conversation was had, I would certainly make notes of any such conversation, but generally I would consider it essential that it be taped, if that was possible. If I didn't have the tape-recording resources open to me, I would make notes and prepare a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. Now, could you look just at that front page. You can look on the ELMO or you can read it. And just go down to line 19 and 20, where you say: "And Mr. Jevtic, you've been interviewed before as a suspect. And I'll confirm again that you're a suspect and you will be treated as such. As a suspect ..." And then you go on to tell him. That starts at 19. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you say that: "Anything you say will be recorded and could be used in evidence in later Tribunal proceedings." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, could we flip to the next page, please. Line 15, you state: "And the interpreter is Adisa ..." I won't mention the name there. Strike that. Probably should have struck that already: "Mr. Jevtic, do you agree that prior to the interview, you had a conversation with myself and Mr. McCloskey"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Jevtic said: "Yes." And you say: "And during that brief conversation, you requested that we have a conversation off tape." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, according to your testimony under oath just now, you would have made notes and made a record of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Where are your notes and then further record of that off-the-record conversation with Mr. Jevtic ?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've only read this page of the transcript in which I say: "Do you agree that prior to the interview, you had a conversation with myself and Mr. McCloskey." I'm not sure if I then continue to discuss that conversation and that, if I did discuss the conversation, would constitute a record of that prior conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let's just flip to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Line 3, you state: "That being the case, I'll suspend this record conversation and the time is 16.59." You also say then: "Okay. This is a record conversation between Dean Manning and Dragan Jevtic, resumed at 17.35"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You had a 36-minute break you had an off-the-record conversation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. By the -- by what's recorded here, we suspended at 16.59 and resumed at 17.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, what was the intention of going off the record before this started and again for 36 minutes? What were you discussing?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the intention prior to the commencement of the interview, because I assumed, and I'm trying to recall, that they said, "We would like to discuss something off the record," and then there was clearly a discussion of some sort. I don't recall that conversation. I would have to check any notes that I made of the conversation and perhaps the rest of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very quickly, I'm about finished: Can you tell me, in your experience in that four years, what are some of the purposes to have an off-the-record conversation like this?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've indicated before that if the person is a suspect, that it would generally not occur. I do recall that many of these people were, to put it mildly, terrified of the consequences of talking to us, terrified that they would be arrested. I recall one occasion a suspect hearing a helicopter outside and thinking that it was coming to arrest them. I don't know, I can't recall, from this brief part of the conversation, what that conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you would agree, sir, that many of these people who you called in as suspects were terrified of the consequences of talking to you, they were terrified of being arrested, and they were so terrified that they were willing to shift the blame from themselves to any other person, and that's normal in a criminal investigation; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You don't?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a complete statement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: As a police officer for 24 years, you've never noticed that people who you interview as suspects want to shift the blame and have a tendency to minimise their culpability and point the finger somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Meek's asked a question in relation to the suspects in this case, and to my recollection, many of the suspects denied any involvement in the crimes. And I said that some were terrified. Some were arrogant, some were frightened, some were thin, tall. They were all different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Some lied to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suspect very strongly that some lied, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And is a part of your job -- is it okay for an investigator to lie to a suspect and tell them something that's not quite true to get them to answer?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I conduct interviews in a fair and honest manner. It is not normal to lie to a suspect or to a witness, and it's my position that if I can, I will tell both suspects and witnesses the truth, if I can. It is not normally my habit to lie to people in any respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I appreciate it's not normally your practice to do that, but from time to time I presume, with your answer, that you will tell suspects certain things; you may not really have a conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, Mr. Meek, stop it. We allowed the first question. He's answered you. Now move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, were you ever involved in the -- as an investigator to conduct Rule 68 compliance?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you have any notes of that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that I made some entries in relation to Rule 68. It was a huge volume of work and interviews. I know that some Rule 68 material was identified by myself. There should be records, notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Now, would they be your notes, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't recall the actual process involved, but -- and I don't want to mislead the Tribunal. I'm sure there was a process involved where we made a record of Rule 68 or at least indicated it to the senior trial attorneys and other attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I just ask, sir, the last question is: Can you generally tell us, what was the protocol, to your recollection, on the Rule 68 compliance?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we -- if I found any material that was clearly or even vaguely exculpatory, then that material should be immediately reported, recorded, and the process would be that it would be advised to the appropriate Defence -- the appropriate area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would the appropriate parties be the Office of the Prosecutor, and then from there, they would turn it over?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Were you recently contacted by another investigator here, Tomasz Blaszczyk, about some documents or notes that you had that you discarded and threw away right before you left in 2002?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have you mixed up with another investigator. I'm sorry. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manning. My name is Ms. Nikolic, and I represent the Defence for Mr. Drago Nikolic. I would like to put to you several questions concerning your investigative work in the Srebrenica case before leaving the Tribunal. So that's the period I'm interested in. From what I understand, you were involved not only in the investigation concerning exhumations, but also in the investigations concerning the ballistics in relation to this case.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Effectively, they were connected to the exhumation process.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Aside from analysing the bullet cases found at the site, was an analysis of weaponry carried out as well from the units that were out in the field, namely, the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, although it wasn't an analysis of the weapons, as such, but the shell cases fired from the weapons, if that's the inquiry you're speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to an analysis of the rifles that were taken from the premises of the barracks of the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigades.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was involved in an operation which seized weapons from the Bratunac and other brigades. Those weapons were then test-fired and the shell cases recovered from those weapons and examined by the ATF. Those weapons were then returned to the relevant units. In that case, we didn't examine forensically the weapon, but the shell case that was produced from that weapon. Perhaps that's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to put to you the answer you gave in the Blagojevic case on page 7209. I've been trying to find the documents from the batch from my learned friends concerning an analysis of around 1.000 rifles that we know was carried out, and I'm referring to the rifles that were taken from the barracks. In answer to Mr. Karnavas' question, you said, Your Honours: [In English] "In a major part of that process, we tried to [indiscernible] from the Bratunac/Zvornik Brigade and other brigades or units in the area of Srebrenica. Those weapons were test-fired and cases were collected with the intention of comparing. That was conducted by Mr. Ols and his associates. Did not recall the ultimate outcome, but I understand it was unsuccessful."

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I agree with that statement, and we are discussing the same matter. To my knowledge, the test-firing produced many hundreds of shell cases. They were examined, and those results were negative. But I wasn't involved in that final part of the process, but I agree with you that they were negative.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, the link between the weapons from the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades and other units and the bullet cases that were found on the Srebrenica mass gravesites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no link was found, to my knowledge, from that test. I caution that by saying something may have changed between now and then, but to my knowledge, there was no link located from those weapons to those shell cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What I should like to ask you now concerns your report, which you must have read closely, dated the 24th of August, 2003. I believe Madam Soljan showed you a map yesterday which was annexed to this report, but in order for you to find it more easily to follow my questions, I will show you only one page of this report, which contains a certain figure, so that we do not find ourselves at cross-purposes. Could I have Madam Usher's assistance in giving this report to Mr. Manning. Before you look at this report, let me ask you this: In your investigative work, while you were collecting the data for your -- today's evidence, you contacted the Cantonal Court in Tuzla, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While you were preparing your report for today and for this particular testimony, you contacted the Cantonal Court in Tuzla, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with their work and their data, are you not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that -- from that visit, I was able to see the files and the way they're structured. I'm not particularly familiar with the laws and the processes in place in Bosnia for domestic crimes, but I -- I reviewed files and became somewhat familiar with their processes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, I really do not wish to go into the domestic law; only the documents that you were shown, records and so on and so forth. Can we call up Defence exhibit 3D265 on e-court, please. While we're waiting for the document, you'll agree with me that before you, you have your report, dated the 24th of August, 2003, that you prepared for your evidence in the Blagojevic case, which was provided to you by Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document we have on e-court. This is the report which, on the 20th of September, 2004, the Cantonal Court in Tuzla sent to the Demographics Section of the Prosecution with the supporting material and tables. Let's turn to page 2, please. Please turn to page 1 of your report, where item number 8 starts. I don't know how we can coordinate e-court and ELMO at the same time, but perhaps Mr. Manning should take the report and place it before him, while the rest of us will be following the document on e-court. Page 1 of the report, 0308 -- I'm sorry, I'm giving you the ERN of the B/C/S version. Page 1, starting with the paragraph: "Summary of the forensic material, 2001 mass graves analysis," item number 8. Mr. Manning, could you please take your findings and place them before you, your report. Look at page 1 and the paragraph -- paragraph number 8, that is.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell me how it starts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This number contains all the bodies found in the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that we don't have the document before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Following that, you have a section where you have the years of exhumations covering the period from 1996 to 2001, and this is the period considered by your report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please look at the screen, where you will see the report of the Cantonal Court in Tuzla for 1996, where you have 224 bodies exhumed in 1996, whereas in your report you refer to at least 479 bodies. In 1998, in your report, at least 895 bodies were exhumed. According to the report of the Cantonal Court in Tuzla, there were 433 exhumed. For the year 1999, as per your report, at least three -- or, rather, 546 bodies were exhumed from mass graves, and according to the report from -- of the Cantonal Court in Tuzla, there were 155 bodies from 40 mass graves. I don't want to go through these figures any further, but please explain to me how you account for these discrepancies, particularly with regard to the fact that the report of the Cantonal Court in Tuzla dates from September 2004.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbers included in my report are from ICTY at that time exhumations. They represent the bodies and body parts located in ICTY graves. This document, to my reading, is data from the Bosnian Commission. I don't know where these figures came from. They're talking 569 graves were opened. Clearly, that's significantly more than the ICTY graves that I have been discussing. I can't really comment on their figures; only to say my figures in my report represent the ICTY exhumed graves and the MNI or minimum number of individuals assessed by Jose Pablo Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document we have on our screens. If you look at the second or third paragraph, where the sources are listed which the Cantonal Court in Tuzla used for this 2004 report, you will see Tuzla Cantonal Court records, Tuzla Cantonal Prosecutor's office record, and the information received from the Missing Persons Institute, which was also used as the source of information by the Tribunal; was it not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see those details. In relation to my report in the Blagojevic trial, I didn't rely on records from the Bosnian authorities. I based the details of that report on data held by ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to page 3 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We have a table here of the locations and mass graves where it says: "Unidentified persons from The Hague graves and other graves." We're looking at the last two columns on the right-hand side. And the text above it says: "Identified: 186 bodies," on the basis of the documentation from the Missing Persons Institute and UKC, and 1.078 bodies exhumed in cooperation with the ICTY. According to the results provided by the Cantonal Court, The Hague graves, or, rather, the graves examined by the ICTY, they are related to 1.078 identified persons. Can you comment on this? Can you give us any further information in addition to what you've already told us?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't reviewed this document. I would note it says "1.078 bodies," not "identified bodies." These records certainly don't -- aren't what I relied on, and I would have to check the underlying material in relation to this. But those figures don't relate to my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Whilst you were preparing your last two reports in 2007, in the months of June and November, you only relied on the ICMP's list, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I relied on the ICMP data in relation to the numbers of identified and the codes relating to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the ICMP sent to the OTP its lists on two occasions to the Demographics Section, which were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Madam Nikolic please repeat the last part of her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you get the interpreters, Madam Nikolic? The interpreters would like you to repeat the last part --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after the Demographics Section of the OTP received lists on two occasions, that corrections and modifications were made there, too, by the Demographics Section?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that two series of data was provided and that the Demographic Unit processed that data and identified some issues, some areas in that material. I didn't thereafter deal with demography and ICMP, but I saw the results of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show 3D267 to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, please read out the first paragraph of this letter sent on the 22nd of October, 2007, to Ms. Ewa Tabeau of the Demographics Section of the OTP. Please read it out loud, since we don't have the B/C/S translation in e-court, we have it only in English.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Dear Ewa. Please find attached an Excel file that accounts for the discrepancies you noted in our previous list of DNA reports relating to Srebrenica. We have broken it into two sheets, one indicating listings for which correction is necessary in the original list, and the second indicating the explanation for the apparent discrepancy, where corrections are either not needed or not possible."

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Does your knowledge on certain corrections tally with what we can read in the document?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read the whole document, but I agree that there were discrepancies identified by Ms. Tabeau. She dealt with ICMP. I saw the results of that inquiry. I examined those results, and I believe in the vast majority, the corrections were not records that affected my report in any way, that is, that they were records which I did not -- did not count or were related to graves and surface collections which I did not deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But that list was the basis for the compiling of your report, the same list?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, the same two lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether all the data from the list is secret, since that information was never disclosed to the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that the ICMP provided that data on a confidential basis to the ICTY. I don't know if they have released that data to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You also are familiar of the mission of the Commission for Missing Persons or, rather, that they are mandated to equally assist the local authorities and courts, particularly in keeping with the contract between the ICMP and the Bosnian government in relation to the work of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, I'm aware that it's part of the three-entity arrangement, if you like. As to their sharing arrangements, I can't comment. I believe that it was envisaged as one commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Manning -- sorry, Ms. Nikolic, a question for the witness. Still referring you to this document that you see on e-court, I just want to have it clear in my mind. The bottom line of that would be that there would be one more in the list or one less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm missing your reference. You're talking about my 2003 report or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, my apologies to you. I'm talking about the document that you were referred to, being a letter from -- or an e-mail from Thomas Parsons to Tabeau -- to Ewa, anyway, Tabeau at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can't see the bottom of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have it -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that entry in relation to that individual, I won't -- perhaps it's not best if I comment on that, because it's not one of the graves that I considered. It's the site or location known as "Kravica," which wasn't an ICTY grave, so I didn't -- I didn't use that data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what I'm asking you, if you look at the paragraph just above the details of the individual, it states: "For one case, the main report was inadvertently left off the list. This is indicated on the sheet, but I append here the relevant information for the main case, to complete the record." So would that be tantamount to adding another individual to the list or revising the list by deleting one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be adding one to the list. A main report is the one that would be counted. The re-associations would form part of that body, so that's one additional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could all background noise please be kept to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. My apologies. My apologies to you, Madam Nikolic, for the interruption. Please go ahead. Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could just request that this image be not broadcasted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has already been taken care of. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A few additional questions, Mr. Manning. In your visit in 2005 -- or, rather, during that visit to Bosnia, I read that you visited the Federal Commission for Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that on that occasion you didn't meet Mr. Masovic. Did you consult the archives of the Commission concerning the exhumations, missing persons, et cetera, or, rather, concerning all the things that were the purpose of your visit?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't consult the archives. I intended to meet with Mr. Masovic, but circumstances meant that I could not. I didn't look at the archives, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you are not familiar with their data, the data they forwarded to the OTP concerning the missing identified people regarding Srebrenica in 1996?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know what data you're speaking about, but I didn't look at the archives. I, as I said, reviewed the material at the Drina, at the re-association centre, and at the Tuzla Cantonal Court. I may have seen some of their data. I don't know specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the Federal Commission has close cooperation with the ICMP as regards Bosnia, and it also cooperates with all of its branches, including the PIP and the other organisations that deal with such issues?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A question concerning the location of the graves that you have been discussing here and mentioning in your reports so far. Concerning the map behind you, I think it is Exhibit 2996, what municipalities are included; Zvornik and Bratunac, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Effectively, it stretches from the village of Pilica in the north to below Zeleni Jadar in the south, and it may take in other municipalities on the map, but effectively the area from Pilica to Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the territory of the municipalities within which these locations are, and how many of such municipalities are there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know generally the municipalities. I'm not that familiar, but I know when I'm in the Zvornik Municipality, but I don't know the boundaries particularly well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In any case, these mass graves do not encompass more than two or three municipalities, i.e., Zvornik and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that they are contained within the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps and that they are located throughout that area. There are graves in the vicinity of Zvornik, there are graves in the vicinity of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please show 3D268 or 1D449. I believe we can use that one as well, if needed, and I believe it was shown to the witness yesterday by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you recall this document? Ms. Tapuskovic showed it to you yesterday. It is a report of the Federal Commission for Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina which dealt with exhumations within a period of time of 11 years, covering 10 municipalities, and they identify 4.515 persons. I went through the lists in detail, and by sheer chance, you had no insight into those. More than 400 persons are mentioned there within the period between 1992 and 1994. Therefore, the figures do not match, again, the figures being presented before this Tribunal. Had you had an opportunity to look at this data before, would your report have been different?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would not have been different, and that is one of the basic reasons why I relied on the ICMP DNA data, because it is a definitive numbering of the individuals. We, in the ICTY, used an MNI. The Bosnian authorities may be counting body-bags or cases. I don't know, and I don't think I should comment further. But the definitive count, it will be available from DNA. Any other count is an assessment, particularly given that the bodies are broken up and that not all the body parts are available.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The Federal Commission for Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Cantonal Court in Tuzla and the rest also used the DNA analysis from the same source you used; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that from this document, and I don't know that from my discussions with them. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Nikolic, even for cutting down your cross-examination to what you did. Mr. Stojanovic. We'll have a break in 10 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Manning. My name is Miodrag Stojanovic, and together with my colleagues, we appear on behalf of Mr. Ljubo Borovcanin. I just wanted to get a few clarifications concerning some things from your yesterday's testimony. Can you tell me, looking at this map, how many were there -- how many mass graves were there in the area of Glogova village?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referring to the map behind me, ICTY graves in the area of Glogova village would be, depending on your definition, Konjevic Polje 2, Ravnice 1 and 2 and Glogova 1 and 2, perhaps even Cerska and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we have on the screen, you need to scroll down, or what appeared on the screen. I think it was a direct shot from the map. Okay. Do you need the map any further, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will have another question concerning this. Therefore, I could ask that we look at the map and focus on the bottom portion. It is P02996. Could we go towards the bottom of the map. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood properly, Mr. Manning, under the geographic term of Glogova village, we can also include the area of the mass graves you termed "Ravnice 1 and 2"; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, taking it that the village of Glogova is on the area near Glogova 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your report dated the 27th November 2007, inter alia, you mention sub-mass graves which you termed "Glogova 7, 8 and 9". Can you explain to us what the notion of sub-mass graves or subsidiary mass graves means? How do you distinguish those from the basic or primary mass graves of Glogova 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Glogova 2 grave is, as you saw on the aerial imagery, an area that was significantly disturbed. When the grave was exhumed, it was found that there were very different features within the grave, and as they exhumed the grave, they would identify that area as a sub-grave. As they progressed, it might turn into part of a bigger grave. It might turn out to be a formation produced by the bulldozer. It might turn out to be a set of tracks through the soil. In the case of Glogova 1, there were very distinct sub-graves. One was dug by a front-end loader and one was dug by a 360-degree machine scooping into the soil, but those formed part of the whole area of Glogova 1 or Glogova 2. We took the decision particularly that we would not attempt to name the sub-graves and perhaps artificially increase the number of graves. Aligned with that was the fact that those sub-graves were all part of the bigger area of Glogova 1 or Glogova 2 or Kozluk, which was made up of three parts of one big digging process, so that's why they referred to sub-graves. And on occasion, a sub-grave might turn out to be a hole dug by a machine with nothing in it. Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: Can you tell us here today whether those sub-graves were dug simultaneously, temporally speaking, or is there a possibility that they were dug in different periods, having in mind the type and depth of the pit, the type of machinery, or any other characteristics you found in the field?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, a number of the expert reports addressed that same question and indicate that the graves or sub-graves were part of the same process in time, very close to each other in time. If you view of aerial imagery of Glogova 2, you can see all those sub-graves are part of the bigger excavation which occurred at the same time. I do, however, know that a grave known as "Grave L" within Glogova, there was evidence that that was created several days after the creation of Glogova 1, and that grave contained the body of 12 individuals bound together in pairs and killed, and shot, each of them in the chest and some in the head. That grave, in particular, was built -- was made some one or two days after the Glogova 1 grave. It, however, was within the boundary of the Glogova 1 graves or grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying, then, that chronologically speaking, it was within a single process; that is, that these sub-graves were created within the course of a few days?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And if I could make it clearer, the Kozluk grave is made up of three graves, and in fact graves 1 and 2 are -- were created when the bulldozer digging grave 3, which is the larger grave, pushed the soil to the side and pushed bodies to the side. So it was made in exactly the same process that created the bigger grave, and it was designated as a sub-grave simply for assisting in processing where the bodies came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you are now referring to Kozluk rather than Glogova, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was giving the example of Kozluk, which is much smaller and easier to describe than the complicated graves at Glogova 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A few words about the graves you termed "Ravnice 1 and 2". Can you tell us or explain to us why those graves were called by using the local geographical term of "Ravnice," although they were in Glogova village? Ravnice, as a geographical feature, is another location.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the grave location was on the Hodzici Road, and on our map it had the term "Ravnice" written in that area. It was simply a matter of that was the name of the feature closest to the grave, and we chose that name. No other reason than that. And it is not in the village of Glogova, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that in fact it is one location, one slope, where bodies were found and that there was no digging of graves, but rather, that some of the bodies that you found there had merely been covered with soil?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This mass grave was found undisturbed; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Your Honours, it had not been disturbed, although it was open to disturbance from natural forms. It hadn't been disturbed by people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were in the field, do you know whether the access road you just referred to is something that heavy machinery could make use of?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We took a bulldozer and rather large trucks through that area. Having said that, the road had clearly deteriorated when we used it in 2001. I can't speak to the condition of the road in 1995, except from an aerial image that I've seen which indicates the road is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, perhaps this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you will be thinking about the need for another site visit to check what you've just asked the witness. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, let us resume at the point where we were talking about Ravnice mass grave. I will be putting questions to you, and then you can say whether you agree or not. Am I right if I say that according to the aerial imagery, the part of the grave you called "Ravnice 1," where the grave was covered up after 30 bodies were buried there, and it was covered up by the soil taken from across the road, whereas down the slope, 157 bodies were found, and this was at the spot that was called "Ravnice 2," and those bodies had not been either buried or covered with soil at all; would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you, although I'd have to check the numbers that you quote. But, yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't mind you checking the numbers, because I'm reading this, but the gist of my question is: According to the aerial imagery dated the 17th of July, it was established that the grave was already created or was being created, if I can put it that way, since it was a process, after all, as you said?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indication on the aerial image of was the soil that had been taken from one side of the road, and that was present on that image. I don't believe that any bodies were visible on that image.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the bodies were brought there after the 17th of July and thereafter as part of a process?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can agree with that without the image in front of me, but the 17th would be when -- up to when that disturbance had been created. So you can say that it was created at some stage before or on the 17th, from that image, but I can't say that it was created after the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You do not exclude the possibility that the bodies, and I'm referring to Ravnice 2, as you termed it, may have been brought at a later stage; you do not rule out that possibility, since the land had not been disturbed there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to, in fact, exclude that possibility from what I know. The grave is referred to as "Ravnice 1 and 2," but it is really one grave, one collection of bodies, the only difference being that the soil was placed on part of the bodies. The definition of "Ravnice 1 and 2" is simply based on when and who exhumed the bodies. There was nothing to indicate that the bodies from one end of Ravnice to the other were from different periods in time. They were consistent in the manner that they were dumped and in the way they were dumped, and also they were very consistent in the artifacts which had been found linking them to the Kravica warehouse. That was -- material was spread right throughout the grave in a relatively uniform manner. So I would have to exclude that they were created on different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the findings of the pathologists involved in the project, Mr. Peccerelli and Mr. Clark, can we agree that the time of death of the autopsied bodies could not be established?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli is an archaeologist, not a pathologist, but the other pathologists, including Dr. Clark, did, I believe, seek to identify a time of death, and one method we utilised was the self-winding watches along with the aerial imagery used to create -- showing the creation of the graves. I would have to check the pathology reports to see if the experts had indicated specific times of death. I certainly cannot recall any indication of a time of death either preceding the fall of Srebrenica or significantly post-dating the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We have had occasion to hear two testimonies here concerning the activities involving the burial of these bodies, and these witnesses said that in the Glogova mass grave, bodies found elsewhere in the areas of the municipalities of Bratunac and Zvornik were buried, and they identified the locations from which the bodies were taken. Is this consistent with your knowledge and experience?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on the testimony of the other witnesses. In Glogova 1, grave L was created after the rest of the grave was created, I think several days, but there wasn't available any other evidence to indicate to me that there were other incidents or depositions of bodies. And I'm trying to think of any statements or interviews to the contrary, but I don't now recall of any other information which led -- which would lead me to think they were put in at different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the data you provided in the report dated the 27th of November, 2007, the total number of bodies found in the primary graves of Glogova 1 and 2 was 370. My question is: Are all these bodies bodies found in the primary graves termed "Glogova 1 and 8" and "sub-graves 7, 8 and 9"; is that the collection that is referred to here?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glogova 2 is -- should be considered as one very large mass grave which was made up of different features. The Glogova 1 grave is a similar picture. Glogova 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 are the same large mass grave known as "Glogova 2." Glogova 1 stands by itself and Glogova 2 stands by itself, with those sub-graves within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The number of identified bodies in your November report, concerning graves Glogova 1 and Glogova 2, is also subsumed by these sub-graves; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the bodies located in Glogova 1 were located in that area of the mass grave. The bodies in Glogova 2 were in that area of the mass grave. And my figures, you must remember, too, are only those identified by DNA, not all the bodies. I'm not sure if I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely my question. We're talking about identified bodies. When referring to Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6 mass graves, which were identified as secondary mass graves, according to the information you had, are you able to say that all the bodies found in those two secondary graves had been transferred from elsewhere or were there whole bodies, allowing for the possibility that for some of the bodies, this was the place of original burial?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some whole bodies within Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6, but I don't believe that they could have been placed in there previously, as that grave wasn't created until September/October of 1995. Had the bodies been collected from elsewhere, there would have been evidence of that difference in the collection of bodies, and one would expect significant decomposition of the body and, from my experience, insect infestations, et cetera, which would have shown a difference in the bodies. There wasn't that type of difference in the Zeleni Jadar 5 and 6 secondary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the partial sanitization of the terrain next to the roadway was carried out in Ravne Buljin [phoen], Kamenica and Pobudje and whether those bodies had been buried anywhere? Do you know if this was the case after the column of the 28th Division and the related events took place?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not specifically aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were bodies in and around the town of Bratunac itself and where those bodies had been buried? I'm speaking in relation to the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not specifically aware of bodies in the area of Bratunac. I'm trying to think back as to the other evidence of killings in Bratunac and at Potocari. No, I don't -- I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the sanitization of the town of Srebrenica was carried out and whether any dead bodies were discovered, and whether and where they were buried, if so?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the dead from Srebrenica were removed. I don't have any details in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there exists any other primary mass grave in the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac, except for Glogova and Ravnice?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the Bosnian Commission graves, Bljeceva, Budak, the grave at Sandici, and that there are other suspect sites around Srebrenica and Potocari and that the work of the Commission continues to identify graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You are not able to say in which of these graves bodies were found that were collected from Srebrenica as a result of the sanitization process?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I don't have any information in relation to the collection of the dead bodies from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you mentioned the grave you referred to as "Sandic." You did not take part in the exhumation process of this grave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in the exhumation of Sandici, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This was done by the Federal Commission in August of 2004, having found 17 bodies as per the report they gave you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be completing my questions, but before that, could we move into private session? I have a document that requires it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that. Let's move into private session, please. One moment. We are not yet in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Yes, Madame Fauveau, if you wish to repeat -- I don't think there is any need for it, but let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, I don't believe I need to repeat anything. Can you show the witness the Exhibit 5D360, which is an excerpt from the interview with Ostoja Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Waiting for this exhibit, can I ask you whether since May 2007 until your arrival here, anyone from the OTP contacted you to know what happened to Ostoja Stanisic's journal, which you photocopied during this interview?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I was asked, some six or so months ago, about an interview. It wasn't about a journal, and I don't recall who it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here in front of you, you have part of this interview with Mr. Ostoja Stanisic, and what you can see on the lower part of this first page, this is his journal or logbook, and Mr. Ostoja Stanisic did show you that part that was important to you. Do you see there is a response from Mr. Ostoja Stanisic stating -- is in this section.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, that part of the interview, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then two lines below, Mr. Ostoja Stanisic said: [In English] "14th, in the morning hours."

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you now remember this logbook or journal which you have photocopied?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no. I accept that I'm indicating there I'm going to photocopy or intending to. I don't have an independent recollection of that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you now page 4 of this exhibit. All along this page, you have asked Ostoja Stanisic to sign each page of the photocopy made of this logbook?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that I say that I would have him sign each page of the notebook, and I do recall -- I do recall a little bit more about that, that interview. I can't remember what the journal was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But later and during the interview, it seems that Mr. Stanisic said: [In English] "The only time I had to make so many signatures was when I was issuing the certificates for children at school." So can we conclude, on the basis of that, that Mr. Stanisic did sign each page of the photocopy of this notebook you made?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that recollection, but I can accept that, from what you've said. I would have to check the copy of the journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, actually, from what we saw, Mr. Stanisic mentioned the date of the 14th, in the morning, but the year is not mentioned in this interview. But one may conclude that part of this notebook concerns the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume so, which would indicate why I was copying it. It may have been of interest in another case, in which case I would have accepted it for another case, but I would accept that it was probably related to Srebrenica. As I say, I can't recall the journal, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you the Exhibit 5D304. This is the notebook of Mr. Stanisic, but Mr. Stanisic told us that it was dated the 17th of May, 2007, page 11, and this is not the journal or the notebook you have photocopied. And I believe you don't speak the Serbo-Croatian language, so you will have to trust me. Can we come back to the first page, please. Here, there is a Cyrillic word "Ostoja," which is Mr. Stanisic's name, his first name. Can we now move on to page 2. Here we have his complete name, "Ostoja Stanisic" in the Cyrillic language. Can we now show page 3 of the document. Can we have the whole page. Here, you can see that there is no signature, and we can look at the whole -- flip through the whole notebook, and there is no signature on any page. Can you accept that this notebook is not the one you have photocopied?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remembering, if you will, that I would have had the photocopies signed, not the notebook. So if this is the notebook, and I don't recognize it, it would be consistent that it wasn't signed. I would have asked for the copies to be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But concerning the notebook of Ostoja Stanisic you have photocopied, you did not take the original copy. He kept the original copy. This is the reason you made photocopies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object. Mr. Manning has indicated that he does not recall the specific interview and whether this is the specific notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau. I think Ms. Soljan is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said he does not remember the notebook, as such, but he didn't say that he does not remember whether he made photocopies or took the original. I don't know. Maybe I can repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you take notebook, did you make photocopies on site, when you took the original notebook from a suspect or an accused or a witness, did you make photocopies on site?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that might vary, but in this circumstance, from reading the brief section of the interview, I would believe that I had copied it then and there, because I asked him to sign it, and he wouldn't have signed the original book that he had. I would not have asked him to sign that. I would have asked him to sign the photocopies that I would have kept and taken presumably back to The Hague. So his -- I would expect his notebook not to be signed; however, the photocopied pages to be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
