utterances.text: Can you tell me what you did with the photocopies signed by Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't, because I don't recall. But had I taken those copies, I would have conveyed them back to The Hague, entered them into evidence. Generally, I wouldn't even -- if on further review they weren't considered of evidentiary value, I would probably still have entered them into evidence as part of the collection of material from that interview, and they would have been stamped and placed into the Evidence Unit, Evidence Section.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And just in order to know whether this has any probative value, you should have used an interpreter or a translator?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't recall the specific circumstances, but, yes, when I was first shown the notebook, I would have asked the interpreter to explain what it was to me. When I returned it into evidence, part of that process is to say, "We need a translation," and perhaps that could have been done verbally or perhaps it would have been, "This document needs to be translated. Please place it in the system and have it translated." And then I would review or someone would review the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you -- had you made photocopies of this newspaper [as interpreted] signed by Mr. Stanisic, would you agree that these photocopies should be somewhere in the OTP's office, a signed photocopy?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would expect them to be somewhere within the Tribunal. I assume you're indicating that they're not. I have no knowledge whatsoever of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, we did not get them. That's the only thing I can tell you. I cannot tell you whether they are in the Prosecutor's office or not. Now, I have another question for you concerning something my colleague has asked you. He talked about non-recorded conversations. That was on page 13 and 14 of today's transcript. And you said that when part of the conversation was not recorded, you would take notes of the conversation. When the conversation was recorded, for instance, a conversation with a suspect, and when, for whatever reason, the recording was stopped, would that part that had not been recorded -- would you have taken notes of that part of the conversation not recorded?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes, I would have, and I think I indicated that before. There are circumstances where I might not. It might be that a person was providing some information in relation to some confidential information. I would probably still record details of that conversation. It might be that they asked me not to make notes. I would probably still make notes at a later time. If I did, those notes would form part of the -- the material that I put into evidence. If it was of a very confidential nature, it might be placed into Rule 70 within the Tribunal or similar. But generally I would take a note of the conversation or I would note that the conversation occurred and what it concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That's all, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madame. I have left the Pandurevic Defence team. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The burial sites which you investigated were divided up by your team into the northern sites and the southern sites; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. That's just an artefact of where they are on the map. We didn't generally refer to them as the northern sites or the southern sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you'll forgive me. I'm referring back to the evidence we had from Mr. Ruez at the very start of this trial where he did divide them in that way. But for my purposes, when I talk to you about the northern sites, I'm talking about the sites within the municipality of Zvornik. You understand what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but would you be able to specify which graves or I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You can turn around and look at the map, but I'm talking about Orahovac, Petkovci, Kozluk and Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That being the primary graves, and the secondary from Cancari Road and upwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm only concerned about the primary graves.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we can go to some aerial images if you want, but will you accept from me that the excavation or re-excavation of those primary graves, those four primary graves, all took place between the 7th and the 27th of September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without checking the imagery, I would accept that the disturbances of the primary and then the secondaries was in September and October, so I can accept that, but -- unless we need to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps you better have them. Can we have P1724 into e-court, please. I'm sorry. These photographs take quite a long time to come up. And this is Orahovac or Lazete, as I think you referred to it at the time of the investigation, and I think these aerial images, you would accept, show a further disturbance of the earth between the two dates which the image providers have placed on the photograph, the 7th and the 27th of September, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that. There also may be other aerial images that have later dates, but I doubt that there would be an earlier date than the 7th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, what I'm going to suggest to you is that all of the images that have later dates relate to sites in a different area of Bosnia. But can we go to P1747, please. I think you looked at this when Ms. Soljan was asking you questions, and you told us that the photograph on the right, the 27th of September, showed that the ground there had been disturbed, according to the aerial image. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So if we take the logical conclusion, not disturbed on the 7th of September, but disturbed by the 27th?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, lastly, can we go to P1763.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, I can't remember whether Ms. Soljan showed you this photograph when you gave evidence-in-chief, but I hope you'll agree that on the left we see some disturbance of the area but, on the right, greater disturbance by the date that the image provider has put on the photograph, the 27th of September?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So in a certain state on the 7th of September, but, according to your analysis of this photograph, re-excavated by the 27th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly disturbed by the 27th. That process may have continued after the 27th, but that image shows the grave being significantly disturbed between those periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I take it from the answers you're giving me that you are happy, as it were, to interpret these aerial images, that you're happy to look at them and state what you think they show?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I certainly am not an interpreter of aerial imagery. Looking at this as a simple photograph, with some knowledge of the lay of the land, I can see clearly that in one image to the other, there is a significant difference. And I know that the marks on the soil there correspond to many of the marks on this image. But I'm not an interpreter of aerial imagery, but as a layman, I can certainly see that within those images.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's not an accidental question, Mr. Manning, because of course we're going to come to some images in a minute where the image providers have put their own commentary on it. Were you ever briefed by the image providers as to who had interpreted these photographs, how they had done it, and by what method, using what techniques?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm conscious that this is or was Rule 70 material. I'm not sure to what level I can discuss that aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Answer this question: Did you ever meet anybody who had interpreted these photographs?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not trying to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This last question, you can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I say, I wasn't sure of the status of the images. I never spoke to or dealt with anyone who actually interpreted the images or put those markings on the images.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like you then to look, please, at P1801, and this is the fourth of the sites in the northern area, Branjevo. Now, you did see this before, and this is a photograph on which, according to you and Mr. Ruez, in fairness, there is some commentary placed by the image providers, and by that I mean it says: "Excavation activity," and on the left-hand side it says: "Newly excavated trench," with an arrow, and then there's a blown-up section in the middle: "Backhoe and front loader." I take it from your previous answer that other than what is written on there, nobody's ever told you how they came to the conclusion that this aerial image showed excavation activity, have they, by which I mean nobody from the image provider?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a conversation with some people who provided this. It's a difficult question to answer, in that if they had access to this image and they saw the machines and the trenches, then that would indicate that they knew there was excavation activity. When these images were presented to me, that was labelled on them, and the provider may have said, "And this shows the trench being dug." The basis for their knowledge of that would have been their knowledge of the image or further down the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't mean to be pedantic, but I wonder if you could just therefore explain the answer you gave at line 17 to 19: "I never spoke to or dealt with anyone who actually interpreted those images or put those markings on the images."

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. I dealt with the next person in the chain. But did I have a conversation with those people? Yes. And to be clear, some of those people may have done that work, conducted that inquiry. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're now at a point, as Mr. Manning has said, where he has talked to someone related to the provider, and that information is protected by Rule 70. And I think that's well understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't think he's going beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I don't think he has, either. It sounds like we're on our way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are getting there, yeah, exactly. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's just concentrate on the image for a while, shall we, Mr. Manning? In the box in the center of this image, there is a horseshoe-shaped track around the farm buildings, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at the top of that horseshoe, there are some farm buildings; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side of the image and at the bottom, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. And we can see going off, as it were, not quite at a tangent, but at a 45-degree angle to the horseshoe, some tracks. You would agree that they're tracks? You told us the other day that they're tracks, and that's presumably something you interpreted and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That track moves from the center of the image to the top left or towards the top left, and I interpret those, from looking at a photograph, as vehicle tracks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, in the enlarged image, we can see that on the far -- well, as we look at it, at the top of the long side of the horseshoe, there is a little collection of objects which somebody has decided to call a backhoe and front loader; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, looking at it yourself, and we do have a facility to enlarge it, is there any way you can tell that that's a backhoe and front loader?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at that image, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you like us to enlarge it a few times to see if it helps?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've gone through that process myself. I believe it shows what looks like a vehicle. I can't say that it's a backhoe or a front loader.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very, very honest of you, Mr. Manning. Now, if we go over to the left-hand side, the image provider has placed there a little commentary box saying: "Newly excavated trench," and do you take that, like me, to be the rather thin, whitish line that's running about north-northwest just between the trees and the ploughed field?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, in fact, take that to be the greater area. When you dig a trench, you take the soil from that trench and generally put it on the side, so that's what I think we're seeing is a trench in shadow and the spoil from that trench, but again that's just me looking at a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's move on, shall we? Can we have a look at P1800. Thank you very much. You'd agree the same area but from a slightly different angle and what appears to be a lower trajectory?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same area, Branjevo Military Farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. But not as high as the other image, not so far above it, it seems. And do I understand your evidence correctly that the yellow writing we see on that image would have been placed upon it by somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Somewhere, presumably, there's a copy of this image without that yellow writing on. Have you seen one like that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we go to the horseshoe again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Top of the horseshoe, just about where the track comes in, do you see an object or a vehicle there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking of the road that runs from the top of the image to the horseshoe, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. It's just in the bottom left-hand quadrant of the crossroads there. You can see it, can't you? Can you see what appears to be a vehicle of some substance there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm assuming that you mean where the top part of the horseshoe meets that road. There looks to be something there. It could be a vehicle. It could be facing the join in the road. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, it's in precisely the same position as the object that somebody called a backhoe and a front loader in the previous photograph, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know. I would have to compare the two. I would also say that from my experience in using those images, because of the angle, some things can be foreshortened. We had some difficulty in locating the graves on occasion, because on the image it looked to be next to a tree; in fact it was some several tens of metres away. But I didn't recognise a backhoe or a front-end loader on that, but then I didn't on the other image.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm having to ask you this because we're not going to hear from the person who made that determination, so you and I are going to have to do our best, and the Tribunal as well. Can we have a look at P1798, please. Now, this is not an aerial image. This -- well, it's not an aerial image in the sense that it's not one that's been provided subject to Rule 70. I'm guessing that this is a photograph taken from a helicopter in which probably Mr. Ruez was flying, and it looks like it was taken in winter. Can you help us as to when the photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right that it was Mr. Ruez in a Black Hawk helicopter. It was perhaps at the end of 1995 or early 1996, in the winter, but from memory I can't recall the exact date. There is another photograph where the helicopter lands at the military farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks very much. It's not the clearest of photographs, but you've been to Branjevo Farm, and in that horseshoe we can see some fairly substantial objects that look like vehicles. One's red and one's green, so far as I can see. Can you see them?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see shapes. I can't, from that, say that they're machines. And I'm trying to recall when I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that's why I pointed out that you'd been there. Were there pieces of substantial farm equipment parked in that area of Branjevo Farm when you went there?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It wasn't used as a pig farm. I don't believe -- I can't remember. I don't want to -- I don't want to say that I can or can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you see other vehicles on the road there and around that yard area in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what looks like two vehicles on the road approaching the horseshoe, I think a blue and another colour. I can't say that the red and the green or blue further on is a vehicle. I would accept that it may be. My recollection of the farm was that it wasn't being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, lastly, can we have a look at P1802, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And on this image, Mr. Manning, I'm really interested in you concentrating on the area at the edge of the wood, just where the ploughed field begins, and the white markings we can see all over the soil there. I mean, pretty much precisely similar to what's shown in the image of the 27th of July, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're going to have to be more specific as to what area you're talking about. You're still talking about the U-shape, the horseshoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the area towards the left-hand bottom corner of the image, where the forest meets the ploughed field, the area which was said to have been evidence of recent excavation.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the gravesite, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We can see there's a similar white line there, similar white areas on this image which appears to have come from a similar sort of recording device as the image from the 27th of July. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an aerial imagery -- aerial image, the same as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you agree that the area that we are concerned about looks pretty similar to the way it did in the aerial image of the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks similar, yes. I can't tell, from this image, if there's any significant difference, particularly given the quality of the previous image, but I accept that that same area has a disturbance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as I've said, Mr. Manning, we're not going to be privy to the techniques or expertise of the person who interpreted the photograph of the 27th of July, but would you agree with me that on the basis of comparing it with other images we've got of Branjevo Farm, the suggestion on the image of the 27th of July that it shows excavation activity is, at best, [Realtime transcript read in error "inclusive"] inconclusive and possibly even fanciful?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't agree with you. I believe that there is a disturbance on that image, and it corresponds to the location of the mass graves that was exhumed in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's only the date I'm worried about. Could it have happened by the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you -- I've missed you. This image on the 17th of July shows a disturbance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's a disturbance that was found to exist on the physical earth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the image of the 27th of July shows no greater or better disturbance than this image shows?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we can say that, but that there is a disturbance on the soil here on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue and before we forget about it, line 20 on the previous page, page 62, "inclusive" should read "inconclusive."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on from this, Mr. Manning, because I did promise I wouldn't be very long with you. What technique did the ICMP use in calculating the MNI?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably didn't. My definition of "MNI" is "minimal number of individuals," which is a term used by the anthropologists specifically involved in a process of counting skeletal remains. ICMP may have used that method in their work. I only dealt with the DNA-based results, which wouldn't be, in my view, described as a minimal number of individuals as a specific term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Even when you are using DNA as a means of investigation, it's important to have a basis for calculating MNI, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if we use the term "minimum number" rather than "minimal," which it's pedantic, but I understood that to be a process used by the anthropologists. But a minimum number of individuals, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Because, let's be perfectly honest, quite a lot of the bodies recovered were actually only parts of bodies, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And unless you have a basis for excluding parts of bodies being counted twice, you can never rule that out, even with DNA, can you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can never rule out what, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, a question was put to you the other day by Ms. Tapuskovic, where she showed you that in relation to numbered bodies that were part of the ICMP results, there were three potential identities. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were talking about what I understood to be related individuals, brothers in this case, or sisters, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, possibly, but equally it could be that where those identities appear more than once in that schedule, it's because different parts of the same body have been recovered, which would naturally have DNA related to that family, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the cases where there was two or three or more possibilities, you have to remember that the DNA protocol would be unique, so you would say that that DNA protocol, whether it be one whole body or ten of that same body's body parts, is unique. It could be that that individual is one of three people, but the key to the uniqueness of the record is that that is a DNA protocol number. If the second brother was tested, he would have a different protocol number, and they would still say that he could be one of his siblings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Precisely. But the converse is equally true, isn't it, that the arm could throw up the DNA that was related to one family, and then a leg could be found which threw up the same DNA, and we cannot rule out the possibility that what is being found are two parts of the same body and they're being recorded twice; that's why we need an MNI calculation?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in DNA, but I can see that that is wrong in respect of the fact that the DNA protocol is unique, even if it was the arm of one brother and the leg of another. The difficulty then lies in matching it to the blood sample provided by the family. That is where the uncertainty as to who it is comes into it. But that arm would come up with a specific type of DNA, and the leg from another individual, even be it his brother, would be again completely different. If you then tried to match those two to the blood sample from the mother or father, you would be able to say, and I'm not an expert, that they are related, that they come from those parents or that parent. But, again, the arm would be unique, and so would the leg. If it's the same body, they would come up with the same code of DNA and be put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that's why we see on that schedule different ICMP numbers throwing up the same possibility for the identity, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same -- the same body throwing up that possibility, but not the same ICMP number. The ICMP protocol number would be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we're going to have to agree to differ on this, but let me move on. Were you aware of the standard used for calculating MNI by Mr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very familiar with the process, as far as a layman can be. Right through the process, I assisted him in his calculation by providing him data.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you aware that the standard used for assessing MNI by Mr. Baraybar was different from that used by Mr. Haglund?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, and I'm not even sure if Mr. Haglund produced an MNI. He may have done, and I wasn't involved in that process with Dr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So in the course of bringing together all these figures, three different standards have been used for calculation, haven't they; Mr. Haglund's, Mr. Baraybar's and the DNA ICMP basis?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my earlier three reports, it was specifically based on the work of Mr. Baraybar, and he may have used -- and indeed he did use records from the 1996 exhumations. My final report for this testimony relies solely on DNA and does not mingle or mix any other counting method. It just relies on the DNA process conducted by ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to turn very briefly to one last topic, which I hope I can do in the next ten minutes. We were talking about the aerial images a little while ago. Did you ever see an aerial image of an execution actually in process or taking place?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And insofar as your involvement in the investigation was concerned, did that actually involve you in the physical exhumation of bodies?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actively participated in the process, but I didn't -- I took a view that I wasn't an archaeologist. I didn't dig, I didn't remove bodies. I certainly carried them. And, generally, if there was an item of interest in the grave, they would call me, they would show me the item. We would discuss it. They would remove it, they would process it. But I was actively involved in that, and once it was recorded it may be that I took possession of the artefact and conveyed it specifically, and then I dealt with them at the mortuary as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you've been at pains, I think particularly when Mr. Meek was cross-examining you, to emphasise how fair, honest and objective you were in conducting interviews with the very many witnesses and suspects you interviewed. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to Mr. Meek that that's the way I conduct my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it's part of your interviewing style to make the suspect or witness perfectly aware of the material at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, again this is quite general, but if I am in a position to tell the suspect certain things, I will. That's not to say that if I have a piece of information, that I will tell that person that I have that information. I indicated I wouldn't lie, but it's not always the case that I would tell them everything that I knew or everything that I had. But, again, that's being very general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what is a lie? Is a lie saying something that's untrue, knowing that it's untrue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You told Mr. Meek yesterday that you remembered interviewing a man called "Milorad Bircakovic." I'm going to show you his interview in a minute so that you can remind yourself of it. Do you remember what position he held within the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. It could have been engineering or it could have been security. I'd have to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He was a driver. Does that jog your memory? He was a driver for a man called "Milorad Trbic".

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you remember the interview sufficiently well to recall whether he was one of those people who was terrified by the process he found himself within, such as you've told us earlier today?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I remember vaguely the interview. If I read the interview, I'd certainly recall now. And if someone was in that state, I would generally -- generally reassure them and say that they had been summonsed. If they asked me if they were going to be arrested, I would say, "No." I would have to read the interview for Mr. Bircakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, I'll tell you just before I show you the interview, he was interviewed as a suspect. Do you recall what basis you had for treating him as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 7D702 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Rather confusingly, Mr. Manning, the first page of this interview is page 2, but life's like that sometimes, and I just want you to have a look at page 2. And the first two or three replies, it's plain from that, isn't it, that Mr. Milorad Bircakovic was unrepresented during the course of this interview, he had no lawyer with him?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he indicates he doesn't have a lawyer, and then I discuss him seeking a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he was told at any stage what, in fact, he was suspected of?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was told that, and I say that from not a recollection, but I cautioned him. I then would have said he was suspected of involvement in the Srebrenica crimes and perhaps detailed what that was. That's generally what I would do. I would -- I would explain to him what we were interviewing him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And Srebrenica crimes, that would mean genocide, presumably, would it?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would mean the Srebrenica investigation. It could be any part of the crimes committed, including the re-burial process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'd like us to go to page 19, please, and conveniently, it's the same in both B/C/S and in English. Sorry, it's been pointed out to me that because it's page 2, it's actually page 18, I think. There we are. It's "19" on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this is what you said to him, and I think you agree with me it's fairly typical of the way you introduced interviews. Can you see about a third of the way down the page, you say: "I'm going to ask you questions about the killings and about organisation for killings of many thousands of men. "Firstly, I want you to understand some things. We have part of witnesses to the killings, we have survivors who were part of the executions, who were shot at, we have aerial images of the executions taking place, we have seized records from the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade, and we've had many people from those brigades and the Drina Corps interviewed. We have your MP logs. "What I want you to understand is that it's very important for you to tell the truth. If you try and hide what happened or hide your part in what happened, or your knowledge of what happened, I can prove that you are lying. And I want you to understand that this is your chance to tell the truth here now. "I have personally exhumed the bodies of thousands and thousands of men and boys from Kozluk, from the Branjevo Military Farm, from the dam above the factory in Karakaj from the Pilica Dom, from the Kravica warehouse, and from Orahovac, and as I said, I want you to answer questions about that." Why did you tell him all that?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, I'm indicating to him that we had a substantial amount of information, that it was in his interest to tell the truth. Clearly, I was conducting an interview. I suspected, as many of them did, that he would lie, and I was trying to give him as much information as possible that we had. Now, I must make comment on two points. I wasn't present for the exhumations at those graves. And you asked me about the aerial imagery of executions, and clearly that's not correct. When I spoke about the aerial image of executions, in the Branjevo Military Farm photographs you can see what I believe and know to be bodies, and I take that as a valid comment, that that image shows bodies that have been executed. And I don't know why I indicated that I personally exhumed those bodies, knowing that I wasn't there in 1996. I would say that I haven't checked this interview against the record, the actual tape, but I accept the majority of what was said there. I can see that there are one or two words missing, but I accept that I said those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you understand the word "hyperbole," Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would that fairly summarise your claim that you had personally exhumed thousands and thousands of men and boys?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from those graves, but I have personally been involved in the exhumation of thousands of men and boys from Srebrenica mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Had you by the 13th of March, 2002?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd been involved in that process since September/October of 1998, when the Zeleni Jadar 5 mass grave was opened, and in that intervening time I was involved in the exhumation of a number of graves, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, you agreed with me earlier, didn't you, that this sort of passage as an introduction to an interview is not unusual for you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in that instance it may be unusual. I can't remember the circumstances as why I felt it appropriate to go into so much detail with this individual. Perhaps because he was a lower-level individual. I didn't perhaps want him to lie and incriminate himself in that lie. Perhaps I wanted to show him that there was a wealth of information available. I don't know that that would be a normal, representative interview conducted by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, using the same adjectives that you used to Mr. Meek, would you describe that passage as fair, honest and objective?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that I said Branjevo Military Farm and Pilica Dom, Kravica warehouse, that's not correct, but, yes, the rest is. We had a significant body of evidence. I was trying to state it as strongly as I possibly could so that this individual would understand that we had a wealth of information and evidence. And as I say, "It's your opportunity to tell the truth."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to finish with this: Do I understand what you're saying correctly, you thought the best way of getting Milorad Bircakovic to tell the truth was to tell him some lies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I didn't follow that, but we'll have a break and I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Well, it's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a break, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, both Mr. Josse and Mr. Bourgon are present in the courtroom. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The problem is, with ending your cross-examination just before a break, is you realise you've forgotten one or two things, but it shouldn't take more than two minutes. So with your leave, can I ask the witness two or three more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we split the difference 50/50?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, we were just talking about interviewing witnesses and suspects. I take it that whether you were interviewing a witness or a suspect, you would regard it as thoroughly bad practice for the interview to take place whilst the both of you were consuming alcohol?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving on, in amongst the many figures you've given us, are you able to give us a figure for the number of bodies that were found, as it were, above ground, on the surface?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure of -- or the number of surface remains is incorporated into the remainder of the Bosnian graves and surface remains. I didn't calculate a specific -- specific number in relation to surface remains specifically because it was difficult to identify exactly where the bodies were located and when, as a collection of surface remains. So, effectively, the surface remains are also -- would also include the other smaller graves or graves exhumed by the Bosnian Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And, lastly, are you aware of the basis upon which the ICMP receives its funding?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that they're funded mostly by donations, but that's the extent of my knowledge. I think Queen Noor of Jordan is involved. There are several notable figures involved, and I think a US politician of some repute was also involved. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you understand that the funding it receives may or is based on sentences of local and international courts?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm completely unfamiliar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Only about five to ten minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you remind the Trial Chamber, has a connection been made between the primary grave of Branjevo Military Farm and a secondary grave?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cancari Road 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could I please ask the usher to put on e-court Exhibit number P01801. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you indicate for the Court what date this image is taken on?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The image is marked "27 September 1995".

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And just briefly, can you describe what is on this image, what you see on the image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Branjevo Military Farm. It's the area of the pig farm, vehicle tracks through the field, and the mass grave at Branjevo Military Farm, also known as "Pilica."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I please have Exhibit P01869. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, can you indicate what the date of this image is?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you please describe what the image depicts?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Effectively, it's the Cancari Road 12 secondary mass grave, and you can see that the tracks leading to the grave and there are vehicle tracks around the grave. It would indicate to me that the grave has been sealed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can we have image P01868 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, what is the date of this image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This image is dated 27 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you describe what it depicts?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows the Cancari 12 secondary grave, and you can clearly see vehicle tracks, what I previously described as a mound of soil next to a trench on the 27th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what is the significance of this mound of soil?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have come from either the trench itself or be on top of the trench.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what does that mean about the grave?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this image, it looks to me that the grave is opened, but it could be that it's being -- been filled in. The lack of vehicle tracks indicate that it's been built.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to image P01610. And this is the last image, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, earlier in cross-examination with Mr. Stojanovic, you were discussing a certain number of graves. Can you indicate to us what this image represents?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This image shows, on the right-hand side of the road, "GL-1", the primary disturbed mass grave, and on the left near the marking that says "GL-2" and "Front loader" is part of the GL-2 mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you, in a little more detail, explain to the Trial Chamber the various sub-parts of the grave that you had been discussing with Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the GL-1 grave, you can see what looked like to be vehicle tracks and soil pushed in a direction. As the grave was robbed, there was a significant movement of earth. That feature you see in the middle of the grave, where those tracks and movements of earth go in a upwards-to-the-left direction, perhaps would have been treated as is separate grave feature by the archaeologists when they dug the grave, so that may have been - and I can't recall - designated grave H. If you look further up to the top right, you see another shape in that grave. Again that would be designated as grave B, perhaps, and in that way they were able to identify the features within the grave as they operated and continued to expand their view of the grave. But if you look at it, it's all part of one grave and there are features within that grave. I'd indicate that the grave L that I spoke of, with the 12 individuals, was next to the house at the bottom of the GL-1 photograph, and that was distinct and separate, but very close to the other graves that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Kwon? Mr. Manning, we don't have any further questions for you. Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would have two questions for the witness arising from re-examination, with your permission, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If they arise out of the re-examination, yes, of course. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, they do arise from re-examination, namely, from the photographs shown to the witness. I will not be going back to the photographs. Rather, I will only use the photograph that we have at present on our screens to save time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, I've got two questions to put to you in relation to this photograph, where we see these labels, "GL-2" and "GL-1" in yellow. Can you tell me, who placed these two yellow labels, "GL-2" and "GL-1"?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You placed them here because, based on the photograph, you can recognise the location at hand; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in the exhumation and identification of both those graves. I knew where they were, and I'm indicating which graves they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the photograph we are looking at now, you also have a label in this white rectangle where it says "Front loader." Can you tell me who placed this label here?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was placed there by the provider of the image.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order not to go back to the other photographs, as it takes time to call them up, do all the photographs shown to you by Madam Soljan and which have labels, have all of them been obtained from the same provider, the provider that gave you these photographs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not appropriate under the Rule 70, to determine which providers we get material from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have misspoken. I didn't want to hear from the witness who the provider was. My question was whether the other photographs, images, shown to us during the re-examination by Madam Soljan were also placed -- those labels, whether they were also placed by the same provider. I don't want to go into who the provider is. I only want to know whether the same labels were placed by the same provider on the other photographs, images.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the objection focuses on the use of -- or your use of the word "same." I think the proper way to put the question is whether the indications on the map which are in white, like we have here on this present photo, were put by the provider, not necessarily by the same provider, because that would just go into what Mr. McCloskey is objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm thinking about that now, and I'm thinking about the authorisation, and I think the provider stands behind all these photographs. So that question is okay, now that I think about it. I apologise. I'm just -- we're just getting close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So basically you have a stipulation there, and you don't need to put the question. You have a stipulation from the Prosecutor, lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case, so there's no point in pursuing the same question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, I am clear now, I should be using the term "provider," but can I get my answer from the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need an answer from the witness. You have a confirmation of what you want to know from Mr. McCloskey, himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I still have one question left for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does the same form of indications in white also apply to the indications of dates, when it comes to these same images?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in these images the yellow text was placed on there by myself. The white text, the label and the date was placed by the provider. In effect, the yellow is mine; the rest is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic. That concludes your testimony. We don't have any questions for you from the Bench. Mr. Manning, I wish, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, to thank you very much for having come over to give testimony. And you have a long journey back home, and we wish you a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will postpone the exhibits till later, and we start with Kingori.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Kingori.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And most welcome. We are about to start your testimony, which will continue in the forthcoming days. Before you do so, you're required by our Rules to - you are familiar with this - to make the solemn declaration. Please read out the text, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. We've got about 20 minutes or 22 minutes to go. Mr. Thayer will go first. Please, Mr. Thayer, I know that you have asked for about three hours. Try to limit it as much as you can. Our idea is that we try and finish the complete testimony of this witness by Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will do my best. I've already cut the examination down. I'll try to keep it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state and spell your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: My name is Lieutenant-Colonel Kingori, and I spell the last name that is Kilo-India-November-Golf-Oscar-Romeo-India.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I'm now 50 years in August this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I was born in Kenya, in Moyale District, and that is where I was raised until I went to Nairobi in 1977 to look for a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let me just briefly review your military service history. You joined the Kenyan Air Force in 1997 and retired this past -- I'm sorry, 1977, and retired this past August at the rank of colonel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is your current assignment or work?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Currently, I'm deployed in Nairobi as the acting director of the National Disaster Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, your service in the former Yugoslavia began in 1994, when you served as an UNMO team leader in Erdut until approximately March of 1995; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you just briefly describe any training that you received to be an UNMO upon your deployment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: First and foremost is that before going to -- for the deployment in the former Yugoslavia, we had a brief in Nairobi concerning what we were expected to do when we got to the operational area. And when we arrived there, that is, in Zagreb, we were trained on various issues that we were going to handle when we were in the field, and that training took about two days, and that involved a lot of things, that is, first aid, things to do with crater analysis, things to do with the reporting, the normal military observer type of reporting, and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in March of 1995, you were assigned to Sector Northeast UNMO headquarters as a member of Team Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where were your offices located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, our offices were located in the PTT building. That was -- I think it was either a postal building or something like that, but that is where our headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were you quartered or billeted?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: We were having our billet in the same place. That is where we were sleeping, that is where we had our offices, and that is where we were doing all our things, like even washing, cooking and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, briefly, would you describe what your team's duties and responsibilities were as UNMOs in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Military observers have, you know, various duties that they are assigned to, but mainly it's to monitor and report any violations to the ceasefire agreement, that is, VCFAs, VCFAs, and also bring the warring factions to an understanding, to bring them together, hold meetings regularly with them in the side, and then so that you can convey whatever you told from this side to the other side and vice versa so you can bridge the differences that hold them apart, and then you can bring them together to an agreement and to a situation whereby they can live together and as one family.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned reporting violations of the ceasefire agreement. Was part of your duties investigating reports of violations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: That is true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe what you would do in connection with those investigations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Now, whenever we went out in case we are told that there is a violation somewhere, we go out in the field, then get the report from the locals or -- so that, I mean, even ourselves, we can see if it is maybe a crater which has hit a certain area, we'll go see the place where the craters hit, analyse the size of the crater, and also the detail that concerns how or where -- from which direction that that shell could have come from, and then get the grid references for the -- so that we can be able to report to the UNMO headquarters through the normal channels. Or if it was maybe some people was injured, we would go there, see them, interview them, and record all the statements from them so that we can be able to transmit the same to our headquarters through the normal channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when you perform these crater analyses, would you use any special equipment for that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was special equipment that we were using, and we had them, and that first and foremost you got to -- the crater, when a crater is formed, it forms in a definite pattern, especially if it has hit a hard surface. It forms in a definite pattern that you'd be able to identify, according to what we had been taught, where the shell could have come from, the general direction of the origin of the shell. Then, with the equipments that we had, you could place them there, on the shelling -- on the hole itself, and then that is the crater, and then be able to measure and know the size or the calibre of the shell. Then you go to the shell, so the fragments that you have there. Then you could be able to check with the documents that we had, because we had a book that carried all the types of weapons which were in that general area. Then you could be able to tell the kind of or the calibre of the weapon. From that calibre, you can be able to identify the range, because all those details are in the book. You can identify the range of that particular weapon. If it is a 155, maybe two and a half kilometres, that is the range. Then from there, you can go to the map that you already have, then try to locate, with the direction that you got from the way the shell landed towards that -- where the source you think could have been, then when you put the two and a half kilometres or so, you be able to identify the general area where the shell could have been launched from.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you just briefly describe the reporting system that Team Srebrenica used?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Our reporting system was just like any other UN military observer teams, in that we had, as a team, to report to our sector headquarters, that is, UNMO's sector headquarters, United Nations Military Observers, not UNPROFOR. So when we report to the UN Military Observer headquarters, that is, sector headquarters, they would now report to the UNMO headquarters in Zagreb, and that is -- that was the normal -- the normal pattern. In fact, we had a very clear way of reporting, and our hierarchy was very definite, in that we still had our own senior military observer in the sector and the chief military observer in the UN headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And your Sector Northeast headquarters was located where, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was located in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, how important was the accuracy of the information that you put in those reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The reports that we used to make definitely were accurate, and that is one of the qualifications of UN military observers, in that the details of whatever they report had to be as accurate as possible. In fact, if there was to be any error, it was actually unforgivable, so we had to make sure the details we put in there were very accurate. That is, when we go out there to maybe check any VCFA and we find any, we will take the task of interviewing the people who were around there. We'd also make an effort to ensure that the leadership in that particular area, you know, is interviewed, and also even people on the other side, that is, the opposing side, is also interviewed so that they can also give us their story from their perspective, and then so that whatever we're reporting is something which is as true as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, how would you indicate, if at all, the different sources of this information and whether or not something was able to be confirmed by you or another member of your team, or where there was something that was not confirmed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: What it is, Your Honour, is that in most cases we are the ones who are doing the investigations, but in case we got maybe a rumour or information from a source that maybe is not that reliable, but for the purpose of writing the report we've got to include that because maybe it could turn out to be true, we always put the initials "NCBU" to mean not confirmed by UNMOs, in that that is what we have had, but for sure we are not the ones who found it, we have just been told. So it would be taken the way it is, and later on you could find out maybe it's true, but if you have not confirmed it, we must indicate it's not confirmed by UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, would you just briefly name, to the best of your recollection, the contacts in the Muslim military leadership that you had in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, Your Honour, the contacts that we had mainly were through Mr. -- the Chief of Staff. That was Mr. Ramiz, and also his intelligence officer. I can't remember his name very well, but there was an intelligence officer. But Ramiz and this intelligence officer were our main contacts with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you ever meet anybody that you understood was the commander of the local military presence?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- I never met anyone that was in charge, only that when I arrived there, that is, in early April, I was told that there was someone who was in charge of the army called Mr., I think, Oric, yes, Naser or Jaser Oric or something like that, but for sure I never met him because by the time I arrived there, he had already left the enclave and his whereabouts were unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you met with Mr. Ramiz -- and do you recall his last name, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yeah, his -- Your Honour, his last name was "Becirovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you met with Mr. Becirovic or the intelligence officer, where would you do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: We would meet either at the PTT building -- in fact, most of the time, we were meeting at the PTT building, but at times, though it was very -- I think it was only once that we met at the opstina, but that was only once. Most of the time we were meeting at the PTT building, at the top. Yeah, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit or see what was told to you was the headquarters of the local military presence?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was -- there was no local headquarter of any military people there, that is, the Muslims. There was just a communications centre, a small communications centre in that same building, but there was no headquarters, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall ever being present in that military -- in that small communications centre? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How many times, and can you recall anything about it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I can remember we had some meetings there, and one of the meetings is when just before -- just before the place was shelled and also even during the shelling is the time we had a meeting with the CO Dutch-Bat there, and also another meeting that we held with the LO Dutch-Bat in the same place, that is, in the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, do you recall anything about the centre? Was it a room, was it a floor; do you recall any details at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The thing I remember is that it was a small room. It was just a small room with some communication equipments, that is, HF, VHF radios, and nothing much, nothing you can call a proper communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What were the topics of your meetings, just generally, sir, with these Muslim military representatives?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This could vary from time to time, but mainly they were calling us for meetings only when they had been attacked by the -- by the BSA, and especially when their people were coming back from Tuzla to bring goods that they had gone to buy there so that they can sell to the people, and mainly is -- if we suspected that these attacks were being caused by maybe disagreements between the two, because in most cases when they were going out, they had to agree with the BSA so that they could be given a safe passage to go out, bring back their goods and all that, but in case there was a disagreement, they were ambushed, they were harmed, and then after that, maybe they would call a meeting and say that they were beaten by, you know, by the BSA. So that's the only time that they used to call us for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive complaints from any other source about shelling or attacks into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of complaints. I think that was normal. In fact, we couldn't stay for long without some complaints coming from the Muslims concerning an attack somewhere, in a certain village, and especially the Bandera Triangle area, which was somewhere to the -- I think to the west or somewhere, and also even in the most of the other villages you could hear attacks, and then, you know, there are complaints that a certain village has been shelled, a certain village there was some shooting from the BSA side, and we would go out that way to investigate that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how often would you verify those complaints, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of the time we could verify. When we arrived there, we could find people who were injured. You could find where a shell has landed. It has exploded and you can see the place. The shrapnel, most of them are there, you can be able to see them. You can even identify the type of weapon used, the injuries on the people, the destruction on the buildings or something like that. You know, you could be able to verify that actually an attack occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did these locations and individuals appear to you to be military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: I didn't get your question well. Are you talking about the ones who attacked or the ones who were attacked?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The ones who were attacked that you were visiting and performing your investigation.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the persons who were attacked were normal villagers. In fact, they were not military at all. As far as we could verify, they were not military, and so their targets were actually civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have interpreters on staff with whom you worked?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did. We had two interpreters who are Muslims, that is, inside the enclave, and we had one who was a Serb from outside the enclave. That is, he was staying in Bratunac, so whenever we wanted him, we could be able to get him. We could call him on radio, get him, arrange for a meeting, and then whatever we wanted, we would discuss in his presence or through his effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the Muslim interpreters, do you know or do you have any idea how long they had been working as UNMO interpreters prior to working with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yeah. When I arrived there, I found these guys there, that is, the two, Amir and Hasan, and those guys had been there for quite some time, at least around three years or so, and that they could give me stories of some Kenyan officers who were there, you know, prior to my arrival there. That was about two to three years or so. And so I had reason to believe that they had been there for about a minimum of three years or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to a Serb interpreter a moment ago. Do you recall the interpreter's name?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Oh, that is someone I cannot forget. His name was Petar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall the names of any Serb military representatives with whom you met with any regularity?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was one that -- who was our main contact with the -- with the BSA military establishment, and that was Major Nikolic. This one was the main contact, and he's the person we met nearly -- nearly always. And whenever we wanted to pass something, he's the guy that we always arranged meetings with, Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were there any other Serb officers whose names -- or whose name you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yeah, there were others, there are others that I happened to meet. Of course, most of them, I cannot remember their names, but at least I can remember there was Colonel Vukovic, there was Colonel, I think, Tricic [phoen], there was -- you know, during my entire stay there, there were people I met. And there was a legal officer, one -- that is during the war. That is the one who told me that he's a legal officer, and his name, Fatim Watamir [phoen] or something like that. I can't remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll get to that in a little while, but just focusing on prior to the July attack, sir, had you met this Colonel Vukovic prior to the attack in July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had. I met him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll leave it there for the day, Colonel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, thank you. We'll continue tomorrow. Thank you, everyone. We'll reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
